description: We're Artemis 26, a two-person team from Ankara working on the Space Mission Design Game challenge. We're building a browser-based game where players design a space mission, manage budget, power and mass, and see how their choices shape the mission's success. Our team is already complete, so we're not looking for new members right now.
summary: Artemis 26 is a pixel-art browser game about designing a small science mission. The player fits a spacecraft from module cards (power, instruments, protection) within a fixed budget and bay, then flies one real week in space: July 2019, autumn 2022 or May 2024. Every asteroid pass, solar storm and flare comes from NASA records for those dates. Each contact can only be recorded by the matching instrument, so what you pack decides what you bring home. After each flight the debrief names what was missed and which module would have recorded it. It addresses the challenge by making players practise real mission design trade-offs: instrument choice against a forecast, budget and volume limits, and power and radiation management.
details:
Play: https://l9nlydoge.github.io/ArtemisXXVI/

What it does: you choose one of three real weeks, read its forecast, and fit a spacecraft from module cards (solar arrays, batteries, camera, spectrometer, radar, particle and high-energy detectors, shielding, magnetic shield, flight computer) within a budget and a fixed bay. The spacecraft launches and flies six legs. On each leg you approach one contact and record it over three to five turns of 30 seconds each, switching instruments on against a limited power supply. Storms bring radiation; if the hull runs out, the spacecraft is lost.

How it works: all events are real. 77 asteroid passes come from NASA/JPL close-approach data, 5 storm legs from DONKI geomagnetic storm, particle and flare records, and 11 planets from the NASA Exoplanet Archive. The DART impact and gamma-ray burst GRB 221009A are checked against NASA pages. The data ships with the game; nothing is fetched while playing.

Benefits: it turns real space data into decisions. Players learn that instruments, power and protection compete for the same money and volume, and that a forecast should shape the payload.

Honesty: asteroid sizes are marked as estimates, representative pictures are labelled as representative, and game costs are stated to be game values, not engineering figures.

Tools: TypeScript, React, Zustand, Vite, Vitest (314 automated tests), Python with Pillow for pixel art, the Web Audio API for synthesised sound.

Use of AI: the idea and the gameplay loop are the team's own. The project is AI-assisted: the code, the interface design, the pixel art and the sound were produced with Claude under the team's direction. The game shows this notice on its Home and Sources screens, and the demo video carries a visible AI mark.
